question.text: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x =e^{2t}, \, y= e^{4t}+6.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}.$
question.explanation:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}. \]

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

\[ x'(t) = 2e^{2t}, \qquad y'(t)=4e^{4t}. \]

Therefore, \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{4e^{4t}}{2e^{2t}} = 2e^{2t}. \]

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2} &= \dfrac{ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\color{black}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\right) }{ \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} \right)}. \end{align*}

Substituting into the formula, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2} &= \dfrac{ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left( 2e^{2t} \right) }{ 2e^{2t} } \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{ 4e^{2t} }{ 2e^{2t} } \\[5pt] &= 2. \end{align*}

question.text: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x = t^2-2, \, y= 2t^4+5$ where $t$ is a real number. Calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}.$
question.explanation:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}. \]

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

\[ x'(t) = 2t, \qquad y'(t)=8t^3. \]

Therefore, \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{8t^3}{2t} = 4t^2. \]

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2} &= \dfrac{ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\color{black}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\right) }{ \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} \right)}. \end{align*}

Substituting into the formula, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2} &= \dfrac{ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left( 4t^2\right) }{ 2t } \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{ 8t }{ 2t } \\[5pt] &= 4. \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Second Derivative of a Parametric Curve

question.text: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x =-\cos t+3, \, y= 2\sin t-1.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}.$
question.explanation:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}. \]

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

\[ x'(t) = \sin t, \qquad y'(t)=2\cos t. \]

Therefore, \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{2\cos t}{\sin t} = 2\cot t. \]

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2} &= \dfrac{ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\color{black}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\right) }{ \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} \right)}. \end{align*}

Substituting into the formula, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2} &= \dfrac{ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left( 2\cot t \right) }{ \sin t } \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{ 2\csc^2 t }{\sin t } \\[5pt] &= -2\csc^3 t. \end{align*}
